gap: No result ChatGPT got puts the makers' PLA bed temperatures side by side: Prusa gives 60 °C, Bambu gives 45–60 °C for its Textured PEI plate, BIQU gives 45–55 °C for Glacier and 30–50 °C for Frostbite. None of them says that the coldest plate, Frostbite, is rated for PLA and PETG only, and retailer listings disagree on whether it also takes ABS.
standout_why: I compared against the two pages ChatGPT cited, plus nozzlenotes.com and 3dadapt.com. Prusa's PLA article (help.prusa3d.com/article/pla_2062) gives 60 °C and recommends satin or smooth PEI. Prusa's sheet guidepost gives no temperatures (its comparison table is an image). Nozzlenotes gives Bambu Textured PEI at 45–60 °C for PLA but names no cold-grip plate. 3dadapt covers only Prusa sheets and gives no temperatures. None of them mentions BIQU CryoGrip or Bambu SuperTack. None puts PLA bed floors on one footing, and none notes that the lowest-temperature plate gives up material range. ChatGPT's answer says textured PEI at '50–60°C' and doesn't mention cold plates.
decides: If the shopper prints only PLA (and maybe PETG), Frostbite runs PLA 15 °C cooler at the bottom of its range than Bambu's Textured PEI (30 vs 45 °C) and 30 °C cooler than Prusa's 60 °C. MatterHackers' table marks ABS, TPU, PLA HR, PVA and nylon as not compatible with it, and it can't be cleaned with alcohol. Anyone who will also print ABS or TPU should take Glacier (PLA 45–55 °C, wide material list) or Textured PEI instead. Our current page lists Frostbite's materials as 'PLA, PETG, ABS'. MatterHackers contradicts that and 3DJake supports it, so the cell should say 'PLA, PETG' with a footnote about the conflict until BIQU's own Frostbite page can be read.
